title: Automatic PMI Cancellation Under the 2026 Housing Order
metaDescription: Learn whether automatic PMI cancellation applies to your loan under the 2026 housing executive order, how current rules work, and what may change.
h1: Automatic PMI Cancellation and the 2026 Housing Order
cardBlurb: The October 2026 housing executive order does not cancel PMI on existing mortgages, but it authorizes a future pilot program for new loans.
introText: The October 22, 2026 executive order does not provide automatic private mortgage insurance (PMI) cancellation for existing mortgages today; it only lets the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) Director direct a pilot for loans made after the pilot is established. Homeowners with existing loans remain subject to current federal rules, which allow cancellation requests at 80 percent of the home's original value or automatic termination at 78 percent of original value.

sections.heading: What the Order Changes and What It Does Not
sections.body:
No. The order cancels no PMI today; it only says the FHFA Director may direct a pilot for loans made after the pilot is established. The White House issued an executive order titled [Decreasing Housing Costs for the American People](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2026/10/decreasing-housing-costs-for-the-american-people/) on October 22, 2026. Section 2(a) provides that the FHFA Director may direct Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac (the Enterprises) to establish a pilot program for single-family mortgages they own, guarantee, or securitize. This pilot applies solely to mortgages made after the establishment of the pilot program, if the Director determines the pilot serves the public and Enterprise interest and is consistent with safety and soundness. The pilot would apply only to mortgages made after it is established.

Section 2(b) outlines three conditions for cancellation under this future pilot. First, the borrower must satisfy applicable equity requirements based on the current market value of the property, which may be determined through an automated valuation model or other approved means. Second, the cancellation must align with financial safety, soundness, and contractual obligations. Third, the borrower must satisfy all other applicable statutory, contractual, regulatory, and Enterprise requirements.

The order omits several operational specifics. It does not publish an exact equity percentage, a distinct payment-history test, or a launch date. Section 4 covers a separate refinance title-insurance change, described below.

sections.heading: How PMI Ends Today Under Existing Rules
sections.body:
While no pilot exists, conventional loan servicers follow standard federal guidelines. According to the [CFPB guidance on removing private mortgage insurance](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/when-can-i-remove-private-mortgage-insurance-pmi-from-my-loan-en-202/), borrowers have two primary benchmarks for cancellation based on original value. Original value represents the contract sales price or the appraised value at purchase, whichever is lower, or the appraised value at the time of a refinance.

Borrowers can request cancellation in writing on the date the principal balance is scheduled to reach 80 percent of original value. You can submit this request early if you make extra principal payments to reach that 80 percent mark. To approve the request, the servicer requires a clean payment history, proof that payments are current, certification that no junior liens exist, and evidence showing the home value has not dropped below original value.

Automatic termination operates on a different timetable. Servicers generally must cancel PMI automatically once your principal balance is scheduled to reach 78 percent of original value, assuming your payments are current. In addition, the servicer must terminate PMI the month following the midpoint of your total amortization schedule, which equals 15 years on a 30-year loan, even if the balance has not reached 78 percent. As noted by the [CFPB explanation of mortgage insurance](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-is-private-mortgage-insurance-en-122/), PMI is generally required on conventional loans with down payments below 20 percent to protect the lender rather than the borrower.

sections.heading: Our Internal Modeling of the PMI Timeline
sections.body:
To show how long borrowers must wait under current original-value rules, we modeled standard amortization schedules for a $400,000 purchase price across various down payments and interest rates. The scope assumes a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage with scheduled payments only, zero extra payments, and original value matching the purchase price. Rates of 5.5 percent, 6.5 percent, and 7.5 percent serve as scenario inputs rather than current rate quotes.

| Down Payment | Interest Rate | Loan Amount | Months to 80% (Years) | Months to 78% (Years) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 3% ($12,000) | 5.5% | $388,000 | 121 (10.1) | 131 (10.9) |
| 3% ($12,000) | 6.5% | $388,000 | 133 (11.1) | 144 (12.0) |
| 3% ($12,000) | 7.5% | $388,000 | 146 (12.2) | 157 (13.1) |
| 5% ($20,000) | 5.5% | $380,000 | 111 (9.2) | 123 (10.2) |
| 5% ($20,000) | 6.5% | $380,000 | 124 (10.3) | 135 (11.2) |
| 5% ($20,000) | 7.5% | $380,000 | 136 (11.3) | 148 (12.3) |
| 10% ($40,000) | 5.5% | $360,000 | 84 (7.0) | 98 (8.2) |
| 10% ($40,000) | 6.5% | $360,000 | 95 (7.9) | 109 (9.1) |
| 10% ($40,000) | 7.5% | $360,000 | 107 (8.9) | 121 (10.1) |
| 15% ($60,000) | 5.5% | $340,000 | 49 (4.1) | 65 (5.4) |
| 15% ($60,000) | 6.5% | $340,000 | 56 (4.7) | 75 (6.2) |
| 15% ($60,000) | 7.5% | $340,000 | 65 (5.4) | 85 (7.1) |

In all 12 modeled cases the 78 percent date falls before the 180-month midpoint, so the 78 percent rule ends PMI first on these inputs. You can evaluate your own schedule by viewing our [mortgage amortization schedule](/mortgage/amortization-schedule/).

sections.heading: Potential Impact of a Current-Value Standard
sections.body:
The order says the FHFA Director may direct a pilot whose equity test would use the property's current market value. While the order names no equity percentage, our internal calculation illustrates how an 80 percent current-value threshold would operate. For a $400,000 home with a 5 percent down payment ($380,000 loan) at a 6.5 percent interest rate, scheduled payments reduce the balance over time while market appreciation adds equity.

Under this illustration, reaching an 80 percent ratio against current market value requires specific property appreciation milestones:

- After 2 years: loan balance is $371,221, requiring a market value of $464,026 (16.0 percent appreciation over purchase price).
- After 3 years: loan balance is $366,386, requiring a market value of $457,982 (14.5 percent appreciation over purchase price).
- After 5 years: loan balance is $355,722, requiring a market value of $444,652 (11.2 percent appreciation over purchase price).
- After 7 years: loan balance is $343,582, requiring a market value of $429,477 (7.4 percent appreciation over purchase price).

Under current rules based on original value, this identical borrower must wait 124 months (10.3 years) for the 80 percent cancellation date and 135 months (11.2 years) for automatic 78 percent termination. If a pilot ever used a current-value test, it could allow earlier cancellation when home values rise. The order names no percentage. Borrowers who made a 20 percent down payment already began at an 80 percent ratio and have no PMI to cancel.

sections.heading: Refinance Title Insurance Pilot Expansion
sections.body:
Section 4 of the executive order addresses closing expenses by permitting an expansion of the title acceptance pilot. If the FHFA Director finds it serves the public interest and financial soundness, the Enterprises may accept an automated title review or approved title-risk assessment in place of traditional lender title insurance. Any expanded program would cover only eligible refinance transactions, which the order does not list.

Under Section 4(b)(i), the Director should consider extending eligibility to refinances with loan-to-value ratios exceeding 80 percent when title risks remain minimal. Section 4(c) says the Director must require that savings be passed through to borrowers, and that lenders inform borrowers of them. The executive order does not state the exact dollar savings or publish which specific loans qualify.

You can explore typical settlement expenses in our guide to [mortgage refinance closing costs](/guides/mortgage-refinance-closing-costs/). If you already have a mortgage and are weighing a refinance, use our [mortgage refinance calculator](/mortgage/refinance-calculator/).

sections.heading: Practical Steps for PMI Today
sections.body:
The 2026 executive order offers no immediate financial relief to existing mortgage holders. Borrowers who put 20 percent down have no mortgage insurance premiums to remove. Meanwhile, if the FHFA Director directs a pilot, borrowers whose loans are made after it is established could become eligible. The order publishes no start date.

If you currently carry PMI on a conventional mortgage, your monthly cost depends on your loan size and insurance rate. Each 0.1 percentage point of annual PMI rate adds $25.00 monthly to a $300,000 loan balance and $31.67 monthly to a $380,000 loan balance. Review your monthly mortgage statement to confirm your current premium charge and scheduled 80 percent balance date.

Borrowers seeking to remove PMI ahead of schedule can accelerate their equity growth by paying down principal. You can test how additional monthly payments pull forward your cancellation date using our [mortgage extra payment calculator](/mortgage/extra-payment-calculator/). Once your loan reaches 80 percent of original value, submit a formal written cancellation request directly to your loan servicer.

sections.heading: Our Takeaway
sections.body:
The [executive order](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2026/10/decreasing-housing-costs-for-the-american-people/) does not cancel private mortgage insurance (PMI) automatically for anyone today. Section 2 only says the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) Director may direct Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to set up a pilot, for mortgages made after it is established. Existing borrowers are not affected, and the only group that could benefit is borrowers whose loans are made after a pilot starts, if the FHFA Director acts. Buyers who put 20 percent down carry no insurance to cancel. The order names no specific equity percentage or start date. Our internal modeling of the PMI timeline, calculated from scenario inputs (a $400,000 price and 5.5, 6.5 and 7.5 percent rates), shows that earlier cancellation would depend on how much the home has appreciated and on the rules the agency sets. This outlook changes only if the FHFA directs a pilot and publishes its terms.

Borrowers must continue using standard cancellation paths under existing rules. Check your loan statement for the 80 percent date against [CFPB cancellation rules](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/when-can-i-remove-private-mortgage-insurance-pmi-from-my-loan-en-202/), then submit a cancellation request to your servicer in writing. Making additional principal payments helps reach that 80 percent mark earlier, which you can track using our [mortgage extra payment calculator](/mortgage/extra-payment-calculator/).

faqs.question: Does the housing executive order cancel my PMI automatically?
faqs.answer: No. The order does not cancel PMI on any existing mortgage. It only lets the FHFA Director direct Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to set up a pilot, and any such pilot would apply only to mortgages made after it is established. Nothing changes for existing loans.

faqs.question: How do I get PMI removed on my mortgage today?
faqs.answer: You can send a written cancellation request to your mortgage servicer when your scheduled or actual principal balance reaches 80 percent of the original value. You must have a clean payment record, be current on payments, and show the home value has not decreased.

faqs.question: At what loan-to-value does PMI automatically end?
faqs.answer: Servicers generally must automatically terminate PMI when your principal balance is scheduled to reach 78 percent of the home's original value, provided your mortgage payments are fully current.

faqs.question: Does the title insurance waiver apply to my refinance?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. The order only lets the FHFA Director direct Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to expand a title acceptance pilot for eligible refinance transactions. It publishes no eligibility rules or start date, so no one can say yet whether a given refinance qualifies.

faqs.question: Will the new PMI pilot apply to loans I already have?
faqs.answer: No. Section 2(a) of the executive order explicitly restricts any resulting pilot program to mortgages made after the establishment of the pilot program.
